desc:
You are given a string s and a list pairs of index pairs [a, b] (0-indexed). For every listed pair you may swap the letters at positions a and b, as many times as you like, in any order, and pairs may be used repeatedly.

Return the lexicographically smallest string that can be produced.

s = "dcab", pairs = [[0,3],[1,2]]         -> "bacd"   (swap 0↔3 to get "bcad", swap 1↔2 to get "bacd")
s = "dcab", pairs = [[0,3],[1,2],[0,2]]   -> "abcd"   (all four positions are linked)
s = "cba",  pairs = [[0,1],[1,2]]         -> "abc"
constraints: pairs[i] = [a, b] with 0 ≤ a, b < s.length
s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: If you can swap positions 0–1 and 1–2, can you also bring any letter of those three positions to any other of them?
Positions connected through chains of allowed swaps form a group, and inside a group the letters can be arranged in any order. Think of the pairs as edges of a graph on the positions.
Find the groups (union-find or DFS). For each group, sort its letters and sort its positions, then write the smallest letter at the smallest position, and so on.
editorial: Adjacent-style swapping along a chain of pairs lets you realise any permutation inside a connected component of the graph whose vertices are the positions and whose edges are the pairs (just like bubble sort moves letters step by step along a path). Letters can never leave their component. So the best string places, within each component, the sorted letters on the sorted positions, which makes every position as small as possible from left to right.

Implementation: union-find over positions to label components, bucket positions by their root (positions are naturally collected in increasing order), sort each bucket's letters, and write them back. Time is O((n + m) α(n) + n log n) and space O(n).
time: O((n + m) * alpha(n) + n log n)
